about: Thin-period fill, batch 2 of 2: the 19 wanted gap items from 239 to 1450 CE (Ram picked them 2026-11-20).

events.name: Queen Himiko Sends an Envoy to Wei China
events.date_display: 238 or 239 (the Chinese record says 238; most historians read 239)
events.description: Himiko, a ruler in the land of Wa in Japan, sends an envoy to the Chinese kingdom of Wei. The Chinese chronicle that records the mission describes her as an unmarried queen who practised sorcery and ruled a country called Yamatai, and says the Wei emperor named her Queen of Wa, Friendly to Wei.
events.note: Recorded in the Wei zhi section of the Records of the Three Kingdoms. The text gives the second year of Jingchu (238); many historians correct it to 239.
events.significance: Himiko is the first ruler of Japan known by name from written records, and her mission is one of the earliest documented contacts between Japan and China. Where her Yamatai lay, in Kyushu or the Nara region, is still debated, one of Japanese history's famous puzzles.

events.name: Pakal the Great Becomes Ruler of Palenque
events.description: At the age of twelve, K'inich Janaab' Pakal takes the throne of Palenque, a Maya city in the rainforest of southern Mexico. In a reign of almost seventy years he rebuilds the city with palaces and temples, and he is buried in a richly furnished tomb inside the Temple of the Inscriptions.
events.note: Accession on 29 July 615, from Palenque's inscriptions; died 683.
events.significance: Pakal's long reign made Palenque one of the leading Classic Maya cities, and his inscriptions are among the longest Maya texts. The discovery of his tomb in 1952, with its jade mask and carved sarcophagus lid, transformed what was known about Maya kingship.

events.name: Arabs Conquer Egypt
events.date_display: 639–642 (invasion 639; Alexandria surrendered in 641 and was handed over in 642)
events.description: An Arab army under Amr ibn al-As takes Egypt from the Byzantine Empire, winning at Heliopolis and capturing the fortress of Babylon near modern Cairo. Alexandria surrenders by treaty, and Egypt becomes a province of the caliphate, governed from a new garrison town, Fustat.
events.note: The story that Amr burned the Library of Alexandria is a later legend: left out.
events.significance: The conquest ended nearly a thousand years of Greek and Roman rule in Egypt and cost Constantinople its main grain supply. Over the following centuries Egypt became largely Arabic-speaking and Muslim, and Fustat, later absorbed into Cairo, grew into a leading city of the Islamic world.

events.name: Borobudur Completed
events.date_display: c. 780–830 (built in stages under the Sailendra dynasty)
events.description: In central Java, builders under the Sailendra dynasty finish Borobudur, a vast Buddhist monument of stone terraces crowned with stupas. Pilgrims climb it in a spiral, passing more than two thousand carved relief panels that tell Buddhist stories, until they reach the open circular terraces at the top.
events.note: Completion usually placed c. 825, in the reign of Samaratungga. Why it was abandoned is uncertain, so the significance doesn't give a reason.
events.significance: Borobudur is the largest Buddhist monument in the world and a high point of the Hindu-Buddhist civilization of early Java. Neglected for centuries after the centre of Javanese power moved east, it was restored in the twentieth century and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.name: Battle of Bạch Đằng Ends Chinese Rule in Vietnam
events.description: On the Bạch Đằng River in northern Vietnam, Ngô Quyền defeats a fleet of the Southern Han kingdom of China. His men drive iron-tipped stakes into the riverbed, lure the enemy ships in at high tide, and attack as the falling tide leaves them stranded on the stakes.
events.note: Late 938. Ngô Quyền proclaimed himself king in 939.
events.significance: The victory ended about a thousand years of rule by Chinese dynasties over northern Vietnam, and Ngô Quyền founded an independent kingdom the next year. The same river saw later victories over Song and Mongol fleets, the last won with the same stake tactic.

events.name: Cahokia Grows into a City
events.description: Near the Mississippi River, across from modern St. Louis, the town of Cahokia grows quickly into a planned city with plazas, wooden sun circles and over a hundred earthen mounds. Its largest, Monks Mound, is the biggest earthwork in the Americas north of Mexico, and the city may hold ten to twenty thousand people.
events.note: Archaeologists call the sudden growth around 1050 Cahokia's 'Big Bang'. Population estimates vary widely.
events.significance: Cahokia was the largest city north of Mexico before the eighteenth century and the centre of the Mississippian culture, whose influence spread across the Mississippi valley. It was largely abandoned by about 1350, long before Europeans arrived.

events.name: Polynesians Settle Hawaii
events.date_display: c. 1000–1250 by recent radiocarbon dating; older estimates ranged from 300 to 800
events.description: Polynesian voyagers, probably from the Marquesas or Society Islands, reach the Hawaiian Islands after crossing thousands of kilometres of open ocean in double-hulled sailing canoes. Navigating by stars, swells and birds, they bring the plants and animals they need to farm and settle these remote islands.
events.note: The settlement date is debated (Kirch; Wilmshurst et al. 2011). Recommend DateFlow-only: a range of over two centuries.
events.significance: The settlement of Hawaii was one of the great feats of Polynesian navigation, made without instruments or writing. The society that grew from it developed into powerful chiefdoms and later the Kingdom of Hawaii, and the revival of traditional voyaging since the 1970s has made it a symbol of Native Hawaiian identity.

events.name: Lalibela's Rock-Hewn Churches Carved
events.date_display: c. 1181–1221 (the reign of King Lalibela; some churches may be older or later)
events.description: In the highlands of Ethiopia, under King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty, workers carve eleven churches down into solid volcanic rock, shaping roofs, windows and columns from a single mass of stone. Tradition says the king meant the town to be a new Jerusalem for Christians who could not make the pilgrimage.
events.note: Tradition credits all eleven to King Lalibela; archaeologists think some may be older or later.
events.significance: Lalibela's churches are among the most remarkable buildings of medieval Christianity and still a living centre of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, which holds services and great pilgrimages there. They show the strength of Ethiopia's Christian kingdom, whose faith went back to Aksum's conversion.

events.name: Polynesians Reach Rapa Nui
events.description: Polynesian voyagers reach Rapa Nui, a small island at the far eastern corner of the Polynesian triangle, more than two thousand kilometres from the nearest inhabited land. Their descendants carve and raise hundreds of giant stone statues, the moai, which represent their ancestors.
events.note: Older estimates went as early as 300–800; current radiocarbon work favours c. 1150–1250. The 'ecocide' story is debated, so the significance presents it as debate. Recommend DateFlow-only.
events.significance: Rapa Nui marks the eastern limit of Polynesian settlement, one of the most remote places humans have ever colonised. Its moai made it world-famous, and debate over what changed the island, from deforestation to the disease and slave raids that followed European contact, has made it a case study for historians.

events.name: Sundiata Keita Wins the Battle of Kirina
events.date_display: c. 1235 (known from oral tradition; the exact year is uncertain)
events.description: Near Kirina, on the upper Niger River, the Mande leader Sundiata Keita defeats Sumanguru, king of the Sosso. The victory unites the Mande peoples under Sundiata, who founds the Mali Empire; its story is told in the Epic of Sundiata, still recited by West African griots.
events.note: Known mainly from oral tradition and later Arabic sources; c. 1235 is conventional.
events.significance: Sundiata's victory founded the Mali Empire, which grew rich on gold and trans-Saharan trade and became one of the largest states in West African history. The epic of his life, passed down by griots, remains a foundation of Mande identity and oral literature.

events.name: Polynesian Voyagers Settle New Zealand
events.description: Voyagers from eastern Polynesia, sailing double-hulled canoes, reach New Zealand, the last large land mass apart from Antarctica to be settled by people. Their descendants become the Māori, adapting a tropical island way of life to a cooler land of forests and giant flightless birds.
events.note: Wilmshurst et al. date first settlement to c. 1250–1300.
events.significance: The settlement founded Māori society, whose culture, language and traditions of descent from voyaging canoes remain central to New Zealand today. Within about two centuries the moa had been hunted to extinction, an early example of people transforming a new environment.

events.name: Majapahit Founded
events.description: On the island of Java, the prince Raden Wijaya founds the kingdom of Majapahit. He first allies with a Mongol fleet sent by Kublai Khan to punish Java, uses it to defeat his rival, then turns on the Mongols and drives them out.
events.note: Raden Wijaya was crowned in November 1293. The flag connection in the significance is hedged ('often linked').
events.significance: Majapahit grew into one of the largest empires in Southeast Asian history, claiming influence over much of today's Indonesia under its minister Gajah Mada. Modern Indonesia looks back to it as a forerunner of the nation, and its red and white banner is often linked to the national flag.

events.name: Tenochtitlan Founded
events.description: The Mexica, a people who had migrated into the Valley of Mexico, found their city of Tenochtitlan on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco. According to their tradition, they settled where they saw an eagle perched on a cactus, the sign their god Huitzilopochtli had promised.
events.note: 1325 is the date in Mexica tradition, widely used.
events.significance: Tenochtitlan became the capital of the Aztec Empire and one of the largest cities in the world, with causeways, canals and a great temple. Spanish Mexico City was built on its ruins, and the eagle on the cactus from its founding story appears on Mexico's flag.

events.name: Kingdom of Ayutthaya Founded
events.description: King Uthong, also known as Ramathibodi I, founds the city of Ayutthaya on an island where three rivers meet, in the central plain of modern Thailand. Well placed for rice farming and river trade, it becomes the capital of a powerful Siamese kingdom.
events.significance: Ayutthaya dominated much of mainland Southeast Asia for four centuries, sacking Angkor and trading with China, Japan, Persia and Europe. It was destroyed by a Burmese army in 1767, and the kingdom that rose after it, centred on Bangkok, became modern Thailand.

events.name: Ibn Battuta Visits the Mali Empire
events.description: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta crosses the Sahara with a caravan and spends months in the Mali Empire, at the court of Mansa Sulayman. His account praises the kingdom's safety for travellers and its devotion to Islamic learning, while criticising customs that he, a strict jurist, disapproved of.
events.note: Left Sijilmasa in early 1352; back in Morocco by early 1354.
events.significance: Ibn Battuta's Rihla is one of the few eyewitness descriptions of the Mali Empire at its height, and a key source for historians of West Africa. It shows Mali as part of a wider Islamic world linked by trade, scholarship and pilgrimage.

events.name: Pachacuti Begins the Inca Expansion
events.date_display: 1438 in the traditional chronology; radiocarbon dates suggest the expansion began some decades earlier
events.description: After defending Cusco against an attack by the Chanka, the Inca prince Cusi Yupanqui takes the throne as Pachacuti, 'he who remakes the world'. He rebuilds Cusco and launches the conquests that turn a small Andean kingdom into the Inca Empire, Tawantinsuyu.
events.note: 1438 is Rowe's chronology, from Spanish-era sources; radiocarbon work (Marsh et al. 2017) suggests Inca expansion started around 1400.
events.significance: Pachacuti's conquests and reforms, continued by his son Tupac Inca Yupanqui, created the largest empire in the Americas before Europeans arrived, held together by roads, storehouses and labour service. It lasted barely a century before the Spanish conquest.

events.name: Machu Picchu Built
events.date_display: c. 1420–1450 (traditionally c. 1450; radiocarbon shows it was in use by c. 1420)
events.description: High on a ridge above the Urubamba River in the Peruvian Andes, the Inca build Machu Picchu, probably as a royal estate for the emperor Pachacuti. Its temples, terraces and houses are made of finely fitted stone laid without mortar.
events.note: Burger et al. (Antiquity, 2021) date occupation from c. 1420. 'Lost city' is a popular label; local farmers always knew it.
events.significance: Because the Spanish never found it, Machu Picchu survived largely intact, one of the best-preserved Inca sites. Brought to international attention by Hiram Bingham in 1911, though local farmers had always known it, it is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and Peru's most famous monument.

spans.name: Kofun Period
spans.date_display: c. 250–538 (conventional; 538 is the traditional arrival of Buddhism)
spans.description: The era in Japan named after the kofun, huge earthen burial mounds, many of them keyhole-shaped, built for the ruling elite. During it the Yamato kings of the Nara–Osaka region extended their power over much of Japan.
spans.significance: The Kofun period saw the rise of the Yamato state, from which Japan's imperial line traces its descent. Close contact with Korea brought ironworking, horses and new crafts, and the arrival of Buddhism at its end deepened Chinese and Korean influence on Japanese culture and government.

spans.name: Swahili Coast Trading Cities
spans.date_display: their peak c. 1000–1500; the towns began earlier, and Portuguese attacks started in 1505
spans.description: The Muslim trading towns of the East African coast, among them Kilwa, Mombasa, Malindi and Zanzibar, which grew rich linking the African interior to the Indian Ocean trade. Their Swahili language and culture blended Bantu African roots with Arab and Persian influences.
spans.note: The span marks their height; Portuguese attacks (Kilwa sacked 1505) ended it.
spans.significance: The Swahili towns tied East Africa into a trading world reaching Arabia, India and China, exporting gold, ivory and enslaved people. They spread Islam along the coast and gave rise to the Swahili language, today spoken by many millions across East Africa.

links.why: Himiko sent envoys and tribute to Wei, one of the Three Kingdoms, and received a royal title.
Himiko's reign came just before the great keyhole mounds; some link her to the early Hashihaka tomb.
Pakal ruled Palenque at the height of the Classic Maya period.
After Abu Bakr united Arabia, his successors' armies moved into Byzantine Syria and then Egypt.
From Egypt the Arab armies pushed west across North Africa, crossing into Spain seventy years later.
Both were Vietnamese risings against Chinese rule; the second, nine centuries later, finally won independence.
Gold from the Zimbabwe plateau reached the coast and was shipped out through Kilwa.
Aksum's conversion founded the Ethiopian church whose faith Lalibela's churches were carved to serve.
The victory at Kirina is the traditional founding of the Mali Empire under Sundiata.
Ibn Battuta saw Mali at its height, under Mansa Musa's brother Sulayman.
Raden Wijaya turned on the Yuan fleet sent by Kublai Khan and drove it from Java.
The Mexica of Tenochtitlan later formed the Triple Alliance that created the Aztec Empire.
Ayutthaya grew into the regional power that sacked the Khmer capital.
Pachacuti's accession and conquests are the traditional start of the Inca Empire.
Machu Picchu was built as an Inca royal estate, probably for Pachacuti.
The Lapita settlers of Tonga and Samoa were the ancestors of the Polynesians who later voyaged to Hawaii.
